speaker_notes.note: ASR alternates between 'Picardo' and similar variants. Jiang is still talking about Piccarda.

interactions.summary: Jiang paraphrases the passage for the class: free will is God's greatest gift, Piccarda gave that gift back through her vow, and the violation is therefore a betrayal of God rather than a minor broken promise.
A student gives a quick but incomplete answer that Piccarda did nothing with her free will.
A student asks whether the real mistake was making the vow at all, and Jiang partially agrees while turning the class toward whether Dante's logic feels too harsh.

claims.claim: Jiang paraphrases Beatrice by saying that free will is God's greatest gift and the proof of divine love for human beings.
Jiang says Piccarda used her vow to give that free will back to God, so human will and divine will become joined like an eternal marriage.
On Jiang's reading, Piccarda's act is not merely failing to keep a vow but betraying God because the vow bound her will to God himself.

A student identifies the disturbing implication that perhaps the original mistake was promising free will to God in the first place, and Jiang grants that this is part of what makes the argument feel harsh.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang translates the vow into an eternal marriage between human will and God.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It gives emotional and juridical force to the claim that betrayal of a vow is betrayal of God rather than bookkeeping failure.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang escalates the vow's seriousness by saying this bond cannot be divorced and cannot be betrayed without spiritual consequence.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the packet's most forceful compression of Dante's severity about vows.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Jiang treats free will as God's greatest gift and as the very treasure a vowed soul gives back to God, which is why betrayal of the vow becomes betrayal at the deepest level.

chronology_notes.note: This packet converts the textual claim about free will into a covenant model: Jiang now explains the vow as returning God's greatest gift back to God, which makes the earlier redemption problem look like broken marital trust rather than mere underperformance.
